extracted.intended_audience: economists, patent policy researchers, intellectual property scholars, and policymakers interested in comparative/historical patent office practice
extracted.subtask_description: Cross-country, historical empirical analysis of patent office practices and institutional features (renewal fees, examination, office discretion) across sixty countries at 25-year intervals from 1850–1999. Focus is on constructing measures of patent policy and testing how those features vary with proxies for information asymmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent renewal fee schedule (ratio of second-half to first-half fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the fees due in the second half of the patent’s life to those due in the first half (expressed in nominal dollars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to summarize the option-like nature of renewal schedules and approximates the ratio of an option exercise price to purchase price. Calculation assumes patent is held to the longest regularly granted period with no discretionary extensions; payments at the midpoint count as second-half. For 1950+, awards assumed two years after application (one year after publication); for 1900/1925 assumed one year after application; for 1850/1875 assumed nominal gap. Tobit and OLS specifications used (Tobit when bounded below by zero). Cases with indefinite extension treated as extendible for 20 years in tabulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of renewal fees paid during patent life
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of renewal fees due over the patent’s life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects frequency of required renewals and hence the menu of patent lives available to patentees. Modeled with a Poisson specification due to ordinal, non-negative character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum delay patentee can request for examination (years)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of years from the application date that an applicant could delay having his patent examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures option for applicants to file unexamined applications that can be activated later; important for strategic filings. Many nations allow such delayed examinations; variable often censored at zero (no delay). Tobit specification used. Footnotes also capture related discretionary provisions (patents of addition, preliminary applications, utility models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count of alternative patent award schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of commonly encountered alternative patent structures offered by a nation (patents of addition, preliminary patents, utility models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures menu of protection forms available to applicants. Modeled with ordered logit. Interpretation: more alternatives imply greater flexibility for patentees. The decline of some alternatives (e.g., patents of addition) in wealthy nations noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office maximum period to extend patent life (years)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of years that patent office officials could extend the length of a patent award without legislative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only includes extensions effected by office officials (not legislative or royal decrees). Because some statutes leave extension length ambiguous, censored regression is used and indefinite/discretionary cases are treated as extendible by up to twenty years for tabulation. Extensions based on pharmaceutical regulatory approval formulas are excluded from this measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office discretion: ability to choose which patents to examine
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether patent office officials have the right to choose which patent applications to examine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of five discretionary powers coded for offices; contributes to a count of office discretion provisions (with others listed separately). Presence increases office control over examination workload and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office discretion: ability to vary fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether patent office officials have the authority to vary the fees charged to the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as one of the five discretionary powers. Can affect the effective price of patent maintenance and the exercise decision by patentees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office discretion: power to license or revoke patents for reasons other than non-working
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the government has the power to license or revoke all or some patents for reasons other than non-working (often applied to pharmaceutical patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counted only when licensing or revocation is possible for reasons other than failure to work the patent. Excludes emergency defense-only licensing. No data for some countries/years noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office discretion: ability to determine the original inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the government can determine the original inventor rather than being constrained to award patent to the first applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discretion affects priority and ownership determinations; coded as one of five office discretion provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office discretion: ability to alter the working period requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patent office can alter the period in which the patent must be worked (i.e., put into practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among the five office discretion items; affects enforcement of working requirements and ability to impose or relax compulsory use conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether patents are examined for novelty (All/Some/None)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorical measure: 0 = no examination for novelty; 1 = some applications examined and/or office rules on oppositions; 2 = all applications examined for novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Middle category includes cases where the office examines some but not all applications or where the office handles oppositions filed by rivals. If no regular examination exists but applicants can request a search, the office is not coded as having examination power. Ordered logit and logit specifications used in regressions; presence of examination implies presumption of validity in many systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition procedures (formal opposition, pre-grant adversarial initiated by office, publication prior to award)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of pre-grant contestation mechanisms: Op (opposition procedure), OpInt (no opposition but office-initiated adversarial priority procedures), OpPub (no opposition but pre-grant publication), OpS (opposition for some applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to capture whether and how outsiders can contest proposed patents prior to grant. Footnotes indicate special cases limited to specific subject matter (food, pharma, military, etc.). In some systems informal oppositions occur; those may not be coded as formal opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference/priority dispute mechanisms initiated by patent office officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether government officials can initiate disputes between rival firms regarding patent priority (interferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked in tables/footnotes (e.g., OpInt). Reflects an office role in resolving priority rather than leaving all disputes to courts or applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant publication of patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether patent applications are published prior to award (OpPub) even if there is no formal opposition procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication facilitates third-party awareness and informal or formal challenges; in regressions publication variants were sometimes grouped with opposition-related categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration systems vs examination systems distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a nation operates a registration system (grant upon formal compliance, courts determine novelty) or an examination system (patent office examines novelty prior to grant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In registration systems, patents are granted following procedures regardless of originality; courts later determine validity, and a presumption of validity often exists where offices examine. This institutional feature is central to analysis of division of responsibilities between offices and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection rule (60 countries, highest 1997 GDP; 25-year intervals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample comprised the sixty countries listed in IMF International Financial Statistics as having the highest GDP in 1997; observations taken at mid-year 1850, 1875, 1900, 1925, 1950, 1975, and 1999; only characterized when the polity was an independent political entity at that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: focus on most economically significant countries; sample is unbalanced over time as new nations gain independence. Special handling for occupations, divided countries, and late independence; use the economically significant portion when a country was divided (e.g., Prussia for pre-unification Germany).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source requirement for patent policy characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of guidebooks/handbooks prepared for inventors/patent agents/lawyers; for each date aimed to identify at least five information sources published within five years of that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendices list sources. Where full data missing (e.g., fees), multiple sources were combined to construct comprehensive measures. Practitioner accounts used to interpret ambiguous statutory practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proxies for information asymmetries
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected proxies used to capture the degree of information asymmetries in the economy: (1) population size, (2) per capita GDP (converted to current US$ and to 1998 dollars), (3) trade intensity = (exports + imports)/GDP, (4) percent employed in agriculture, (5) literacy rate (ability to read and write).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability: population (99% obs), GDP (91%), trade intensity (92%), agriculture (81%), literacy (71%). GDP conversion: use PPP-based deflator if possible, then convert to 1998 dollars using US GDP deflator (back to 1889) or US CPI for earlier years. Proxies imperfect; interpret with caution due to inconsistent definitions across countries/time and measurement error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control variable: legal family classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Control for the family into which a nation’s commercial laws fall (La Porta et al. classification) with adjustments for communist regimes and an 'other' category for distinct systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two adjustments: pre-communist legal families used for observations before communist takeovers; countries with unique pre-modern legal systems (e.g., Japan pre-1889) coded as 'other'. Dummy variables for legal family used in regressions (coefficients not reported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding assumptions for award timing and fee calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumptions about timing of award/publication relative to application used to allocate fees into first vs second half: 1850/1875 nominal gap, 1900/1925 awards one year after application, 1950+ awards two years after application (one year after publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These timing assumptions affect which payments count as first-half vs second-half in ratio calculations. Payments happening on midpoint date are counted as second-half. Cases where awards measured from publication or award date required practitioner assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of ornamental design registrations from patent measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries that only had provisions for registering ornamental designs (often called design 'patents') were excluded from patent measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: design registrations resemble trademarks/copyrights more than patent awards and would confound measures focused on invention protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of pharmaceutical/regulatory-based patent extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent life extension measures do not include cases where pharmaceutical patents are extended by a formula based on the duration of regulatory approval processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such formula-based extensions are excluded to keep the measure focused on administrative discretion rather than statutory regulatory compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of colonies, occupations, and divided polities
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation recorded only for independent political entities; colonies without independent patent policies often omitted; in special cases (e.g., West Germany 1950) observations included when independent patent systems were adopted prior to end of occupation; for divided countries, policy from the economically significant portion used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: many colonies registered patents from colonizers or had no patent policies. Examples: used Prussia for Germany pre-unification; used West Germany after WWII; Iraq and Taiwan handled with special source treatments where IMF data missing or political status ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions about coding indefinite extension powers
rubrics_metrics.description: When patent officials’ discretion to extend patents was not limited to a set number of years, those cases were treated as having the right to extend awards by a period equal to the longest statutorily specified patent extensions in any country (twenty years) for tabulation purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pragmatic cap was applied for comparability in tables and regressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and measurement caveats for literacy rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Literacy measured as percentage of population with basic literacy skills, defined by UN Demographic Yearbook as the ability both to read and to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This measure is imprecise, especially for older periods and developing nations, and should be interpreted cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory/interpretive rubric linking institutional features to information asymmetries
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical predictions used to interpret institutional features: where information asymmetries between government officials and patentees are greater (larger populations, richer economies, more trade), policymakers provide patentees more discretionary features (renewal fees, delayed examination), but limit patent office discretion and divide responsibility for patent validity between office and courts when collusion risks are higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the guiding hypothesis for variable selection and interpretation: e.g., steeper renewal fee schedules and more frequent renewals indicate greater patentee discretion; lower office extension powers and increased judicial role indicate attempts to limit bureaucratic discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods: model choices for different variable types
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of regression/specification: Tobit for bounded dependent variables (e.g., fee ratio bounded below by zero), OLS where appropriate, Poisson for count of renewals, ordered logit for ordinal counts (e.g., count of alternative patent schemes or measure of office discretion), censored regression for maximum patent-life extension, ordered logit/logit for examination involvement outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model selection justified by distributional nature of dependent variables; standard errors reported and significance levels noted. Nation or legal-family fixed effects used in select regressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of missing or sparse country-year data
rubrics_metrics.description: When official data were missing (e.g., GDP, fees), alternative sources or consensus estimates from press/government publications were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Iraq GDP gap filled with consensus press estimate; Taiwan data obtained from government publications due to IMF omission. Many demographic variables had missingness and thus were used only in some regressions.
